title: Labor has no answer on weak productivity
full_text:
Jim Chalmers and Anthony Albanese have been exposed for using the cheap trick of increased population in an attempt to boost lacklustre economic growth. And the RBA is not happy about it.
After giving the Labor government some relief by holding off a fourth interest rate rise this year, the Reserve Bank then whacked the pair by saying the bank’s slight upward revisions to below-trend GDP was nothing more than population growth.
“Relative to the May forecast, a stronger population growth assumption has led to slightly higher GDP growth over most of the forecast period,” it said.
It then hit them again by downgrading the government’s key priority of productivity. And it downgraded productivity forecasts not by a little bit but by a significant margin.
Productivity in the December quarter has been revised to minus 0.5 per cent, down from the previous forecast of 0.2 per cent. In one quarter, there’s a 0.7 per cent reversal – or an entire year’s worth of what Treasury ambitiously assumed productivity could be.
“The board also remains concerned about the continued weakness in productivity growth. And continued weakness will constrain the economy’s ability to grow without generating high inflation,” the board said.
Asked if the RBA was concerned that the only thing lifting GDP slightly was population growth, governor Michele Bullock’s response was clear: “Are we concerned? Yes, we’re concerned because the productive capacity of the economy is not growing,” she said on Tuesday.
More frightening for the bank is the fact that it has had to revise up the next four quarters of government spending.
This spending is what is driving GDP and guess what’s driving government spending? Population!
The RBA statement on Tuesday estimated population growth in the December quarter would be 1.4 per cent, up from 1.2 per cent in the previous forecast. By June next year, the population will grow at a higher rate than previously thought.
“Public demand is expected to continue supporting growth over the forecast period … the small upward revisions to the forecast largely reflecting stronger population growth,” it said.
The problem is that while population increases, and GDP goes up a bit, the lack of productivity means people work harder for less and that shows up in per-capita GDP.
“The outlook for GDP per capita in 2026 has been revised down,” the bank said. The problem with productivity is the level of business investment that actually contributes to GDP. Data centres have driven all the increase in business investment; but so much investment is just imported machinery so there is not much addition to real GDP.
Might the government’s tax changes to capital gains – where plenty of investors and businesses will have to pay higher effective tax rates, pushing them out of high-growth companies that reinvest – be part of poor productivity forecasts?
The RBA says it doesn’t have a responsibility explaining the impact of tax changes on business investment. It involves too much uncertainty, too much government legislation, and would affect only a part of aggregate demand. “Our expertise isn’t in business taxation and potential impacts and incentives,” Ms Bullock said.
Yet the RBA does seem to be an expert on data centres. It has provided dozens of insights into data centre investment and the impacts they have on the economy. Surely data centres carry just as much uncertainty as controversial government legislation, and only affect a part of aggregate demand too? There are some things the government is happy for the bank to talk about.
